What is the publication status on the percentage of non-Hispanic black children aged 8–17 with elevated blood pressure, United States, 2013–2014 (NHANES; Table I)?
response_text:
**Suppressed.** The 2.0% estimate for non-Hispanic Black children fails the NCHS Data Presentation Standards for Proportions and would not be published.

**Why, walking the criteria:**

| Check | Value | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Effective sample size ≥ 30 | 145.3 | pass |
| Events > 0 and ≠ denominator | yes | pass |
| Degrees of freedom ≥ 8 | 13 | pass |
| Absolute Korn-Graubard CI width | 6.1 pct pts (0.3–6.4) | > 5 pts, so relative width must be checked |
| **Relative CI width ≤ 130%** | **305.0%** | **fail → suppress** (table footnote 6) |

The estimate is statistically sound on every sample-size and design criterion; it fails only on precision. A 95% interval running from 0.3% to 6.4% is more than three times as wide as the point estimate itself, so the estimate cannot support a substantive reading.

**Two consequences worth carrying forward:**

- **The complement is publishable.** Normal-or-borderline blood pressure for the same children is 98.0% with the identical 6.1-point absolute width, but a relative width of 6.2% — well under 130%. It would be presented, carrying footnote 7: a note that its complement does not meet presentation standards. Same data, same interval, opposite publication status.
- **Non-Hispanic Asian children (0.9%, relative width 566.7%) are suppressed on the same ground.** The Hispanic (2.5%, 108.0%) and non-Hispanic white (0.5%, 320.0%) rows differ — note that the white estimate *passes* here despite an RSE of 58.0%, because the proportions standard uses Korn-Graubard interval width rather than the RSE > 30% rule, which would have flagged it as unreliable.

So a race/Hispanic-origin comparison of elevated blood pressure from this table can only be made between Hispanic and non-Hispanic white children; the Black and Asian cells are unavailable.
